extraction.name: CommonsenseQA
extraction.description: A commonsense question-answering dataset containing 12,247 multiple-choice questions generated by crowd-workers from ConceptNet concepts. Each question has five candidate answers, including one correct answer and four distractors, and is intended to require background knowledge without a supplied context. Retrieved Google search snippets provide additional context for experiments with reading-comprehension models.
extraction.creator: Alon Talmor; Jonathan Herzig; Nicholas Lourie; Jonathan Berant
extraction.citeAs: Alon Talmor, Jonathan Herzig, Nicholas Lourie, and Jonathan Berant. CommonsenseQA: A Question Answering Challenge Targeting Commonsense Knowledge. arXiv:1811.00937v2 [cs.CL], 15 March 2019.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The authors extracted ConceptNet subgraphs containing one source concept and three target concepts linked by the same relation. Amazon Mechanical Turk workers authored three questions per subgraph, each selecting a different target as the correct answer while excluding the other two. Workers added two further distractors per question, and a separate group verified question quality. Google search was queried with each question concatenated with each candidate answer; the first 100 result snippets per candidate were collected, yielding 500 snippets per question. A total of 16,242 questions were formulated, resulting in 12,247 final examples. There were 122 question formulators, and the total cost per question was $0.33.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis; Manual Human Curator; Software Collection
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: ConceptNet, a graph knowledge base containing 32 million commonsense triplets, supplied source concepts, target concepts, and relations. Additional raw content consisted of questions and distractors authored by Amazon Mechanical Turk workers and result snippets retrieved from Google search.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Triplets sharing a question concept and relation were grouped into sets of three distinct answer concepts to produce semantically related candidate answers. Each question received another distractor selected from ConceptNet concepts sharing the relation and one manually authored distractor. For a separate SANITY experimental condition, the difficult distractors were replaced with random ConceptNet distractors.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: ConceptNet triplets were filtered to exclude general relations such as RelatedTo and relations already well explored in NLP such as IsA, leaving 22 relations. Triplets were also excluded when either concept exceeded four words, was not in English, or the edit distance between the two concepts was too low. This produced 236,208 triplets and approximately 43,000 question sets comprising 130,000 triplets. Generated questions were retained only when at least one of two verifiers selected the intended correct answer; this verification step filtered out 15% of questions. The final dataset was split 80/10/10 into training, development, and test sets, using both uniformly random splits and splits with disjoint question concepts.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers were shown a question concept and three answer concepts, but not the ConceptNet relation. They authored three questions containing the question concept, each answerable by one target concept but not the other two, and were instructed to avoid words strongly associated with the correct answer. Workers added one ConceptNet-derived distractor and one manually authored distractor that should appear plausible but be easy for humans to dismiss. Only question formulators whose questions passed verification at least 75% of the time were accepted. A disjoint, trained group of workers verified questions by marking them unanswerable or selecting the correct answer. For dataset analysis, 100 randomly sampled development examples were manually annotated with potentially multiple commonsense skills, averaging 1.75 skills per question.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Each generated question was checked by two verifiers and retained if at least one selected the intended correct answer. This filtered out 15% of questions. For a separate human-performance evaluation, five workers uninvolved in question generation answered each of 100 randomly sampled questions, and majority voting was used to determine the answer per question; reported human accuracy was 88.9%. Commonsense-skill analysis allowed multiple skill categories per question, so category frequencies did not sum to 100%.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: Two human verifiers per generated question. A separate human-performance evaluation collected five answers per question for 100 randomly sampled questions.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Although 122 workers contributed questions, 10 workers formulated more than 85% of them. The dataset's ConceptNet relation distribution was uneven: AtLocation accounted for 47.3% of questions and Causes for 17.3%. An analysis of 100 development examples found surface clues hinting at the correct answer in 35% of examples. The authors state that freely generated questions often require knowledge seldom explicitly reported on the web because of reporting bias.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The quality-verification protocol required agreement with the intended answer from only one of two verifiers. In an analysis of 100 development examples, questions with a correct answer of finer granularity than a distractor constituted 31% of examples, and 35% contained surface clues to the correct answer. Retrieved web snippets did not yield high reading-comprehension performance, suggesting that they carried little useful information for the task. Question formulators were not shown the originating ConceptNet relation and sometimes asked questions probing other relationships, so source relations do not necessarily identify the knowledge needed to answer a question.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, development, testing, and fine-tuning of commonsense question-answering and natural language understanding models. The dataset supports evaluation with or without retrieved web-snippet context. The authors provide 80/10/10 training/development/test splits using both random assignment and disjoint question concepts, designate the harder random split as the primary split, tune hyperparameters on the development set, and evaluate test-set accuracy. The dataset is intended to facilitate research on incorporating commonsense knowledge into NLU systems.
